elements.content:
• Why HTML is the foundation of web pages

• Course objectives and learning outcomes

• Structure of the upcoming lessons

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Ms. Clara Hart, and I’m thrilled to welcome you to our Introduction to HTML course. Over the next few weeks we’ll build real web pages together, step by step.
First, let’s look at why HTML is the foundation of every web page. HTML provides the structure—think of it as the skeleton that holds all the content together.
Next, our course objectives: by the end of this class you’ll be able to write valid HTML tags, create page layouts, and publish a simple personal website.
Finally, the structure of our upcoming lessons: we’ll start with basic tags, move on to lists and links, then explore images and forms, wrapping up with a mini‑project.
That’s our roadmap for today—let’s dive in and start building the web together!

elements.content:
• Doctype declaration

• <html>, <head>, <title>, <body> tags

• Simple complete page example

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
<title>Page Title</title>
</head>
<body>
Content goes here
</body>
</html>

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into the basic structure of an HTML document.

First, we always start with the doctype declaration, which tells the browser that this is an HTML5 document. Then come the opening <html> tag, followed by the <head> section where we place metadata, and finally the <body> where all the visible content lives.

Here’s a simple, complete example: we declare <!DOCTYPE html>, open the <html> tag, add a <head> with a <title>, and then the <body> with any page content. This minimal skeleton is the foundation for every web page you’ll build.

elements.content:
• h1–h6: define document hierarchy

• <p>: paragraph block

• Accessibility: clear structure, semantic tags

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let’s dive into the building blocks of HTML structure: headings and paragraphs.
First, the heading tags h1 through h6 create a hierarchy for your document. Think of h1 as the main title, h2 as a section subtitle, and so on down to h6, which is used for the smallest sub‑headings.
Using this hierarchy not only helps readers scan your page, it also gives screen‑readers a clear outline, which is essential for accessibility.

Next, the 

 tag is the standard way to group sentences into a paragraph. It adds spacing automatically and tells browsers and assistive technologies that this block of text is a distinct thought.

A quick best‑practice tip: always start your page with an

actions.topic: Why is heading hierarchy important for accessibility?

questions.question: Which HTML heading tag should be used for a main section title on a page?
questions.analysis: The <h1> tag represents the top‑level heading and is used for the main title of a page. <h2>–<h4> are for sub‑sections.

elements.content:
• Create hyperlinks with <a href="...">...

• Embed images using <img src="..." alt="...">

• Consider security (avoid unsafe URLs) and SEO (use descriptive alt text)

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Ms. Clara Hart, and today we’ll dive into two essential HTML elements—links and images. By the end of this slide, you’ll know how to create clickable hyperlinks and embed pictures safely and effectively.

First, the anchor tag <a href="…"> lets you turn any text or image into a hyperlink. The href attribute holds the URL you want to link to, and you can add optional attributes like target="_blank" to open the link in a new tab.
Next, the image tag displays pictures on your page. The src attribute points to the image file, while the alt attribute provides a textual description for accessibility and SEO benefits.
Finally, remember security and SEO best practices: always use absolute or trusted URLs, avoid linking to malicious sites, and write meaningful alt text so search engines understand your images.
That covers the basics of hyperlinks and images. In our next activity, you’ll practice adding both to a simple web page. Let’s get coding!

elements.content:
• Ordered list <ol> with items <li>

• Unordered list <ul> with items <li>

• Nesting lists for complex outlines

actions.text: Let's start with the basics: an ordered list uses the <ol> tag, and each item inside it is marked with <li>.
Here you can see an example of an ordered list. Notice how the numbers are generated automatically, and each bullet point is wrapped in <li> tags.
Now, moving to unordered lists: we use the <ul> tag, but the individual items are still <li>.
This snippet shows an unordered list with bullet points. The browser renders circles by default, but you can style them differently with CSS.
Finally, you can nest lists inside each other to create complex outlines—just place another <ol> or <ul> inside an <li>. That lets you build hierarchical navigation menus easily.

questions.question: Which HTML element is most appropriate for creating a navigation menu that links to the main sections of a website?
questions.analysis: The <nav> element semantically defines a block of navigation links. <section> groups related content, <article> represents a self‑contained composition, and <aside> is for tangential content.

questions.question: Consider the following HTML image tag. Which statements are true? (select all that apply)

options.label: The image lacks an alt attribute, which is required for accessibility.
The width attribute sets the display width of the image.
The src attribute should include an absolute URL for the image to load.
The tag is self‑closing and valid HTML5 syntax.

questions.analysis: A is correct because alt provides alternative text for screen readers. B is correct; width defines displayed width. D is correct; is a void element and does not need a closing tag. C is incorrect; a relative URL is acceptable.

actions.text: Alright, let's dive into a quick quiz to see how well you’ve grasped the basics of navigation menus and image markup. Read each question carefully and think about the key points we just covered.

Remember, the <nav> element is designed specifically for grouping navigation links, while <section> and <article> are for thematic content, and <aside> is for tangential information. Choose the most appropriate tag for a main site menu.

For images, always include an alt attribute for accessibility—it’s not optional. The width attribute controls how wide the image appears on the page, but the src can be a relative path; it doesn’t have to be an absolute URL. And in HTML5 the tag is self‑closing without a slash.
Take a moment to answer the questions, then we’ll review the answers together. If anything feels unclear, just let me know!

elements.content:
• Build tables with <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td>

• Create forms using <form>, <input>, <label>

• Accessibility: add scope to <th>, use label with for attribute

actions.text: Alright, let’s dive into our Tables and Forms Overview. We’ll see how to structure data with tables and gather user input with forms.
First, building a table uses the <table> element as the container, <tr> for each row, <th> for header cells, and <td> for regular data cells.

Here’s a simple example:
NameAge
Alice30
. Notice how the tags nest to create rows and columns.

Next, forms let users submit information. Use <form> as the wrapper, <label> to describe each input, and <input> for the actual fields. For example: <form><label for="name">Name:</label><input type="text" id="name" name="name"></form>.
A quick accessibility tip: always pair <label> with its corresponding <input> using the “for” and “id” attributes—screen readers will then read the label correctly.
That covers the basics of tables and forms. Feel free to experiment by adding more rows or input types, and we’ll build on this in the next slide.

elements.content:
• Sectioning tags: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Meaningful headings (<h1>-<h6>) and descriptive alt text for images

• Consistent indentation, clear comments, and HTML validation

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let’s dive into Semantic HTML and why good coding practices matter.

First, we have the sectioning tags: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. These elements describe the purpose of each part of our page, making it easier for browsers and assistive technologies to understand the structure.

Next, always use meaningful headings—like <h1> for the main title and descending <h2>, <h3> for sub‑sections—so the hierarchy is clear. And don’t forget alt text for images; it provides a text description for users who can’t see the picture.
Finally, keep your code tidy: proper indentation, helpful comments, and run it through a validator. Clean code is easier to read, debug, and maintain.
That covers the key points for today—sectioning tags, clear headings and alt text, and solid coding style. Great job, everyone!

questions.question: Which HTML5 semantic element is most appropriate for the main navigation links of a website?
questions.analysis: The <nav> element specifically defines a set of navigation links. <header> is for introductory content, <section> groups related content, and <aside> is for tangential content.

questions.question: Select all form controls that are suitable for collecting a user's preferred contact method (multiple selections allowed).
questions.analysis: Checkboxes permit multiple independent choices, which fits a user who may want more than one contact method. A drop‑down can also allow multiple selections when the 'multiple' attribute is used. Radio buttons allow only a single choice, and file input is unrelated.

questions.question: Explain why using semantic HTML tags (such as <article>, <section>, <nav>, and <footer>) is important for web accessibility and SEO.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Improves accessibility for assistive technologies - 40%; (2) Provides meaningful document structure for search engines - 35%; (3) Enhances code readability and maintainability - 25%.
questions.analysis: A good answer should mention that semantic tags give screen readers clear cues about page regions, help search engines understand content hierarchy, and make the markup easier for developers to read and maintain.

actions.text: Alright everyone, it's time for our final knowledge check on HTML5 semantics and form controls. You'll have a single‑choice question, a multiple‑selection question, and a short‑answer prompt. Read each carefully and remember the key points we covered: choosing the right semantic tag for a page region and picking the appropriate form element for user input.

For the first question, think about the element that specifically describes a set of navigation links. That's the tag we use to wrap menus, site‑wide navigation bars, and any list of links that help users move around the site.

The second question asks which form controls are suitable for letting someone pick their preferred contact method. Remember, checkboxes allow multiple selections, radio buttons enforce a single choice, and a drop‑down list can also present several options. A file input is for uploading files, not for selecting a contact preference.

The short‑answer question wants you to explain why semantic tags like <article>, <section>, <nav>, and <footer> matter for accessibility and SEO. Think about screen readers, document outlines, and how search engines understand page structure.
Take your time, apply what you've learned, and once you're done we'll reflect on how these concepts fit into building accessible, well‑structured webpages. Great job getting this far!
